links.note: Turns 'adding 10 to a number gives 20' into x + 10 = 20. Translating a number statement into an equation is the first half of using linear equations on a problem.
3x = 20/7 - x carries the variable on both sides, so what moves across is the term -x, not a constant. That a variable term may be added to both sides is the new idea this concept supplies.

2x + 3 = 2(x - 4) reduces to 3 = -8, so NO value of x makes the two sides equal and the answer is that no root exists. The item is about what a solution is - the only one in the chapter where there is none.
Writes the smallest of three consecutive numbers as x - 1 given the largest is x + 1. Setting up the algebra for a number problem.
The next even number after x is x + 2 - expressing a number relation algebraically before any equation is solved.
The odd number just below an odd x is x - 2, not x - 1. The same setting-up step for a number problem.
With a difference of 21 and larger number x, the smaller is x - 21; 21 - x is offered as the reversal trap. Expressing the relation is the work.
A two-digit number with units x and tens y is 10y + x. Place value written algebraically, the setup step for digit problems.
-2/3 = 2x is solved by dividing both sides by 2 to get -1/3. One operation performed on both sides, leaving the balance undisturbed - nothing is transposed.
3y + 4 = 5y - 4 has the variable on both sides; subtracting 3y from each is subtracting a variable term rather than a number, giving y = 4.
(2x - 1) + (x - 1) = x + 2 has to have its brackets opened and collected to 3x - 2 before anything else can be done; simplify first, then solve.
11x - 5 - x + 6 = 2x + 17 collects to 10x + 1 = 2x + 17, then 2x is taken off both sides - a variable term, not a constant, moved across.
Complementary angles differing by 10 give x + (x + 10) = 90 and a smaller angle of 40. A geometry-flavoured application of a linear equation.
Supplementary angles, one double the other: x + 2x = 180 gives the larger as 120. Forming and solving the equation is the whole task.
Two numbers differing by 3 and summing to 23 give x + (x+3) = 23, x = 10, so 13 and 10. A standard number application. NOTE: the marked key (12, 11) is wrong - see report.
Five consecutive naturals summing to 65 put the middle one at 65/5 = 13, via x-2 ... x+2 summing to 5x. A consecutive-number application.
x + 12 = 9(x - 12) gives x = 15 - an age problem, which this concept names among the applications alongside number and perimeter problems.
3/(x+8) = 4/(6-x) has to have the fractions cleared by cross-multiplying before anything can be transposed; choosing that first move is what makes the rest routine.
Two numbers in the ratio 3:8 summing to 165: 11 parts give 15 each, so 45 and 120. A ratio application solved by a linear equation.
Sum 69 and difference 17 give 43 and 26. A two-condition number problem reduced to a linear equation.
Denominators 3, 2 and 6 are cleared by multiplying through by 6, their LCM, which is precisely this concept's example; then 20x = 20 and x = 1.
Picks ax + b = 0 against quadratic, cubic and quartic forms. What separates them is that the highest power of the variable must be one.
x^2 - 2x + 1 = x^2 - 3 has its squared terms cancel, leaving degree 1. The subtle case of the highest-power test: a squared term present does not by itself stop the equation being linear.
